title: The Rashtriya Rifles: The temporary force that stayed 36 years
text: Indian Army's Rashtriya Rifles The Rashtriya Rifles was raised as a force that could be wound up by executive order. Thirty-six years later, it is among the Indian Army âs most decorated formations. Indian governments have a particular talent for the permanent temporary arrangement. The Calcutta tram, which has spent most of my adult life apparently months away from abolition, is one example. The Rashtriya Rifles is another, though rather better armed. When it was raised on 1 October 1990, with six battalions - three sent to Punjab, three to Jammu and Kashmir - the RR was constituted under a provision of the Union Composite Table that allowed it to be disbanded by executive order. Thirty-six years, roughly 63 battalions and a budget line of â¹12,052 crore for 2026-27 later, the order remains unsigned. On Thursday (October 1), then, the force marked its raising day as what it has quietly become: routinely described as the largest counter-insurgency formation in the world and, for a generation of Kashmiris born or brought up after 1990, among the most visible faces of the Indian state, sometimes more visible than the state itself. A force nobody particularly wanted to pay for The proposal for a dedicated counter-insurgency force went to the government in 1988, and even the question of who raised it has the faintly comic quality of a file that passed through too many desks. A 2017 Defence Ministry release credits General V.N. Sharma. Most histories give the credit to General S.F. Rodrigues, who was chief when the force was actually raised. The name that recurs most consistently, however, is General B.C. Joshi, whose idea it was and who, after becoming chief, pushed its expansion to 36 battalions by 1994, the year he died in office. Its first Director General was Lieutenant General P.C. Mankotia. The original design was a hybrid. Only a quarter of the men were meant to come from the regular Army; the rest would be ex-servicemen and lateral inductees from the paramilitary, somewhat in the manner of the Assam Rifles. That is not what happened. The Rashtriya Rifles became, and remains, an all-Army force: officers and jawans on deputation, drawn on an all-India, all-class basis from virtually every arm and service, serving tenures of roughly thirty months before returning to their parent units. The money was messier still. Since internal security fell under the Home Ministry, the Home Ministry initially paid for the RR. By the time that arrangement ended in 1997, it reportedly owed the Army â¹950 crore for raising and equipping the force. From 1998-99, the Defence Ministry took the bill onto its own books; the allocation that first year was â¹263 crore. The Home Ministry, meanwhile, had questioned whether the force should exist at all, arguing that its creation amounted to accepting that internal rebellion had become a permanent feature of Indian life. It remains one of the more clear-eyed sentences produced by any ministry on Kashmir, and among the more comprehensively ignored. What the borrowed soldiers did The RRâs finest hour is probably the one almost nobody remembers. In the summer of 1999, while the country watched the ridgelines of Kargil, 26 RR units held the Valley and another three guarded the Banihal and Jawahar Tunnel approaches. Roads remained open. Lines of communication remained usable. The war on the heights could therefore be fought without the Valley unravelling behind it. There is, unfortunately, no battle honour for a highway that stays open. The structure of the force explains much of the method. An RR battalion carries six rifle companies rather than the infantryâs four, leaves much of its heavy weaponry at base and, unlike a regular unit rotating between stations, remains tied to the same terrain: the same district, villages, orchards, roads and families. Five Counter Insurgency Force headquarters â Victor, Kilo, Delta, Romeo and Uniform â divide the territory between them. The rifles, in that sense, are only part of the inventory. The other asset is accumulated memory: which family had a son disappear in 2016, which hillside trail is usable after the snow, which village argument is merely a village argument and which one means somebody ought to pay attention. By the forceâs own 2015 tally, it had neutralised 16,368 militants: 8,522 killed, 6,737 apprehended and 1,109 who surrendered. The latter two figures deserve more attention than they usually get. Nearly half the men in that total were either captured alive or surrendered. Counter-insurgency is often narrated through body counts because body counts are simple, but a man who gives up his weapon is, in several respects, the more interesting outcome. By its 27th raising day in 2017, RR personnel had received 7 Ashok Chakras, 34 Kirti Chakras, 238 Shaurya Chakras and 1,637 Sena Medals. Names on the ledger One of the more complicated arguments for the RR model was made by a man who had once stood on the other side of it. Nazir Ahmad Wani, from Cheki Ashmuji in Kulgam, had been a militant before surrendering and joining the Territorial Army in 2004. In November 2018, operating with 34 RR at Batagund in Shopian against six heavily armed Hizbul Mujahideen and Lashkar militants, he continued fighting after being mortally wounded and killed two of them. He became the first Kashmiri to receive the Ashok Chakra. His widow, Mahajabeen, accepted it at the Republic Day parade. Five years later, in September 2023, the price was paid in a single morning in the Gadole forests above Kokernag. Colonel Manpreet Singh, commanding 19 RR and four months from the end of his tenure, Major Aashish Dhonchak, who left behind a two-year-old daughter, and Sepoy Pradeep Singh died alongside Deputy Superintendent Humayun Bhat of the J&K Police. Bhatâs father, himself a retired police officer, laid a wreath on his sonâs coffin. Two uniforms, one forest. It is worth remembering, especially in the easy shorthand of conversations about Kashmir, that the Kashmiri policeman has spent these decades in the same line of fire. Some names travelled further. Major Mukund Varadarajan of 44 RR became the subject of the Tamil film Amaran in 2024. Others travelled less: Naik Dilwar Khan of 28 RR, killed in Kupwara in July 2024, was awarded the Kirti Chakra the following January. An anniversary piece that mentions the medals must mention something else as well. A force that has operated among civilians under AFSPA for thirty-six years cannot be the sole author of its own report card. Kashmir keeps a ledger too, and not every entry in it is a citation. A country confident about its institutions ought to be capable of reading both without pretending that one makes the other disappear. The quiet handover The unwinding has, in fact, already begun, in the manner Indian institutions generally prefer: gradually, administratively and without anybody standing at a lectern to announce that history has changed direction. In 2021, the RR headquarters moved from Delhi to Northern Command in Udhampur, and its chief was downgraded from lieutenant general to major general. A year earlier, after Galwan, Uniform Force had been moved to Ladakh to face a considerably more conventional adversary. After the Pahalgam attack of April 2025, the Defence and Home ministries began discussing the movement of RR battalions out of the hinterland and towards the Line of Control, with the CRPF taking a larger internal-security role. Three CRPF battalions were moved into Udhampur and Kathua as part of that process. Last month brought a more concrete step: around 2,100 CRPF personnel and at least nine CoBRA teams are to take over 21 sensitive locations across those two districts, operating from existing Army camps. Reports have been equally careful to point out that a substantial RR presence will remain. The budget, meanwhile, continues to rise. In May, the Army began procuring 159 bullet-proof troop carriers for RR units, capable of operating at altitudes of up to 5,000 metres. A force preparing to disappear does not usually buy new vehicles. The better description, therefore, is probably redeployment rather than withdrawal: away, slowly, from the orchard and towards the frontier. That is a sensible direction, but nearly everything depends on the pace. Retired officers who support the shift have also cautioned against pulling RR battalions out abruptly, because what the CRPF needs to inherit is not merely a camp. Camps are easy. There are registers, stores, maps, keys and handover notes. Thirty-six years of village-level memory is rather harder to put into a folder. The Army can transfer the barracks. It cannot transfer an informerâs trust. General Joshi built the Rashtriya Rifles as a bridge, meant to carry the state across a crisis for which it had not prepared. Bridges sometimes remain standing long after the emergency that required them, partly because they continue to be useful and partly because institutions, like people, become reluctant to give up arrangements that work. Usefulness is not the same thing as permanence. The most meaningful raising-day gift for the Rashtriya Rifles would therefore not be another parade or another citation. It would be the slow, careful fulfilment of the possibility written into its creation in 1990: that there might come a day when the force was needed less. Not because it had failed, but , in enough places, it had done what it was raised to do.

title: Khairatabad seat falls vacant as Telangana Gazette notifies turncoat Congress MLA Danam Nagenderâs disqualification
text: The high court's judgment has led to the formal disqualification of Danam Nagender as an MLA representing the Khairatabad Assembly constituency (Photo credit: X) HYDERABAD: The Telangana Gazette has formally notified the disqualification of Danam Nagender as MLA from the 60-Khairatabad Assembly constituency, following the Telangana High Court judgment dated September 18, 2026. The notification, published in the Telangana Gazette on September 26, states that Nagender stands disqualified as a member of the Telangana Legislative Assembly with effect from April 23, 2024, under Paragraph 2(1)(a) of the Tenth Schedule read with Article 191(2) of the Constitution. Consequently, the Khairatabad Assembly seat stands vacant from the same date, news agency ANI reported. The notification, issued by Telangana Legislative Assembly Secretary Rendla Thirupathi, was issued pursuant to the high court judgment in writ petitions Nos. 8409 and 8647 of 2026. The high court had disqualified Nagender after holding that he had contested the 2024 Lok Sabha election from Secunderabad as a Congress candidate while being a BRS MLA. The court also set aside the Assembly Speakerâs decision dismissing petitions seeking his disqualification, ANI reported. The Supreme Court subsequently upheld the high court order, dismissing Nagenderâs plea challenging his disqualification. The apex court held that there was no ground to interfere with the high courtâs order. Reacting to the Supreme Court verdict, Telangana BJP president N Ramchander Rao had described it as a victory for democracy and constitutional morality. He demanded that MLAs who had joined the Congress resign and seek a fresh mandate through by-elections. The Gazette notification now formally records Nagenderâs disqualification and the vacancy of the Khairatabad Assembly seat with effect from April 23, 2024. title: Brace for protests today at Jantar Mantar
text: New Delhi: Delhi Police has not granted permission for a protest called by student groups, civil society activists and opposition parties at Jantar Mantar over the functioning of the poll panel, chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. title: Operation Sheruwali: How security forces tracked LeT commander Musa in months-long hunt since May
text: Hashim Moosa (Left) killed in an encounter in Jammu and Kashmirâs Budgam district, Indian Army (File photo) NEW DELHI: The killing of senior Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) commander Mohammad Asif alias Hashim Musa in Jammu and Kashmir's Budgam district on Wednesday was the culmination of a months-long intelligence-led operation, named âOperation Sheruwaliâ, launched in May 2026. Security forces had been tracking Musa for a prolonged period before a coordinated plan involving multiple agencies was drawn up to neutralise him, following the receipt of technical and human intelligence about his movements and presence in the area. The operation culminated in an encounter in the Yousmarg area of Budgam, where Musa was killed. His body was later recovered along with war-like stores, according to the Army. Also read| Ex-Pakistan SSG commando, highly trained LeT terrorist, Pahalgam mastermind: Who was Hashim Moosa; killed in J&K encounter The ministry of information and broadcasting said the operation dealt a blow to the LeT network in Jammu and Kashmir, with Musa's killing bringing an end to a group of four senior commanders who had been operating in the union territory since 2022 and were linked to several attacks. Watch Operation Sheruwali Intensifies In Rajouri As Army Tightens Cordon Around Suspected Militants How Operation Sheruwali unfolded According to a statement issued by the Press Information Bureau (PIB), security forces had been pursuing Musa for a long time. A specific plan involving all stakeholders was recently put in place after intelligence inputs indicated his movement and presence. The government said the operation to neutralise Musa was part of the ongoing âOperation Sheruwaliâ, which began in May 2026. The Army's Chinar Corps, meanwhile, said the encounter took place during Operation Korag in the Yousmarg area of Budgam district. Troops launched a search operation based on specific intelligence inputs and challenged suspicious movement, following which terrorists opened fire. The operation involved the Indian Army, Jammu and Kashmir Police and the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF). The search continued after the encounter, with security personnel checking the surrounding areas for any additional terrorist presence. Musa's body was recovered from the general area of Palmaidan along with war-like stores, according to the Chinar Corps. Is Hashim Moosa an ex-Pakistan SSG commando? One of the key aspects of Musa's background is his alleged association with Pakistan's military. ANI, quoting security agency sources, reported that Musa had served as a para-commando in Pakistan's Special Service Group (SSG), where he held the rank of Havildar. According to the sources, he retired from the SSG in 2023, subsequently joined the LeT and infiltrated into India. Former Jammu and Kashmir DGP S P Vaid described Musa as a highly trained commando specialising in ambushes and guerrilla-style attacks. Vaid alleged that Musa's footprints had been seen in several attacks in Jammu and Kashmir, including those in Poonch, DKG, Bhimber Gali, Gulmarg and the attack on pilgrims in Reasi. However, his alleged military background has been reported by security agency sources and has not been independently established. Four-member LeT group neutralised With Musa's killing, all four senior LeT commanders belonging to the group that had been active in Jammu and Kashmir since 2022 have been neutralised, according to the government. The three other commanders were killed in separate encounters: Junaid Bhat: Neutralised on December 3, 2024, in Dachigam. Suleman: Killed on July 28, 2025, during Operation Mahadev. Yasir: Neutralised on September 4, 2026, during Operation Asdhar. The government linked the group to several attacks across Jammu and Kashmir, including the Halan attack in August 2023, DKG attack in December 2023, Kandi attack in May 2023, Shahsitar attack in May 2024, Shiv Khori attack in June 2024, Gagangir and Bootapathri attacks in October 2024, and the Baisaran attack in April 2025. Musa's alleged role in Pahalgam attack Musa was among the key suspects in the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terror attack , in which terrorists targeted tourists at Baisaran Valley, killing 26 people. The Jammu and Kashmir Police had announced a reward of Rs 20 lakh for information leading to the arrest of Pakistan nationals and LeT terrorists Adil Hussain Thoker, Ali Bhai and Hashim Musa. The National Investigation Agency (NIA) subsequently chargesheeted seven accused in the case, including Pakistan-based LeT and The Resistance Front (TRF), which it accused of planning, facilitating and executing the attack. title: Jharkhand officials rush to resolve 11.8 lakh electoral roll claims
text: Ranchi: Jharkhand has entered the most demanding phase of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, with 882 election officials racing to dispose of nearly 11.8 lakh claims and objections before the Oct 14 deadline set by the Election Commission (EC). The bulletin on SIR issued by the CEO office revealed that 11,79,761 applications have been received under Forms 6, 6A, 7, and 8 by Sept 30. If all remain pending, officials would need to dispose of an average of 84,269 applications a day over the 14-day window, ending Oct 14. Chief electoral officer (CEO) K Ravi Kumar on Thursday said, âA total of 882 ERO and AERO officers have been deployed for the exercise.â The bulletin does not specify how many applications has been disposed of by Oct 1. The Sept 30 deadline witnessed a last-minute surge, with 59,666 applications filed on a single day, including 34,820 Form-6 applications for fresh enrolment and 24,106 Form-8 applications for corrections. The final-day tally also included 739 Form-7 deletion requests and one Form-6A application. Fresh enrolments account for the bulk of the workload at 6,92,597 applications, followed by 4,73,609 Form-8 correction requests. Form-7 applications number 13,443, while 112 applications were received from overseas electors under Form 6A. The pressure is uneven across districts. Ranchi recorded the highest final-day intake at 7,662 Form-6 and Form-8 applications, followed by Giridih (5,905), Dhanbad (4,099), East Singhbhum (3,455), and Hazaribag (3,213). Within Ranchi district, Hatia (2,112), Kanke (1,641), and Khijri (1,272) accounted for the highest volume of final-day applications. The final electoral roll is scheduled for publication on Oct 19. CEO Kumar reiterated that under SIR-2026, voters who have received notices generally do not need to visit the ERO office for hearing. In cases of no mapping or logical discrepancies, BLOs will go door to door, collect required documents from voters in light of the notices, and upload them on ECINET, enabling the ERO to decide as per rules based on available facts and documents. Many voters have submitted documents, while some voters registered in the 2024 electoral roll and who filled enumeration forms could not complete the hearing process. Such voters should be identified through special outreach programmes and camps, he added. If any voter voluntarily reaches the ERO office or designated hearing venue, the officer concerned must be available. Special attention must be given to PVTG, Divyangjan, tribal groups, elderly voters, workers, the poor, the homeless, and voters whose parentsâ details are unavailable. Voters may call 1950 for assistance, the state CEO stated. Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news. Download the TOI App.

title: No Khairatabad bypoll notification until pending poll plea resolved: ECI tells HC
text: No Khairatabad bypoll notification until pending poll plea resolved: ECI tells HC Hyderabad: The Election Commission of India (ECI), on Thursday, informed the Telangana High Court that it would not hold a by-election in the Khairatabad Assembly constituency until a pending election petition filed by Congress leader P Vijaya Reddy is resolved. The seat fell vacant following the high courtâs disqualification of MLA Danam Nagender in an order on Sept 18. Ironically Nagender, is now a Congress leader. He had won the Khairatabad seat in 2023 on a BRS ticket, then contested the Secunderabad Lok Sabha seat the next year on a Congress ticket resulting in his disqualification by the high court, which was subsequently upheld by the Supreme Court . The commission's submission was made before a division bench comprising Chief Justice Aparesh Kumar Singh and Justice Vakiti Ramakrishna Reddy during the hearing of a lunch motion moved by Congress leader and former GHMC corporator Vijaya Reddy who finished as the runner-up in the 2023 polls, behind Nagender. She had previously filed an election petition seeking to declare Nagenderâs election null and void and recognise her as the winner. This was last listed before a single judge in July 2025. Representing the petitioner in the present petition, senior counsel Vedula Venkataramana argued that SC precedent prohibits treating a seat as a âcasual vacancyâ while an election petition seeking a declaration of victory remains pending. Further, citing Sections 84, 98 and 101 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, he contended that the ECI lacks the legal authority to declare or notify a by-election for the Khairatabad seat while the outcome of her legal challenge is pending. Concurring with the argument, ECI standing counsel Avinash Desai assured the court that âthe seat would not be declared a casual vacancy until the election petition reaches final adjudicationâ. Taking note of ECIâs stance, the bench directed the Commission to submit a formal affidavit confirming that no by-election notification will be issued in the interim and adjourned the case to Oct 6. Meanwhile, after Nagenderâs disqualification, Vijaya Reddyâs counsel moved an interlocutory application (IA) before the single judge requesting to have the election petition taken up and decided on a day-to-day basis so that the truth would come out and she would have the opportunity of being declared the successful candidate in the Nov 2023 polls. This will enable her to serve as MLA until the end of Dec 2028 in the interest of justice, failing which she would suffer serious loss and damage, she said in the IA. In Jan 2024 Vijaya Reddy filed the election petition alleging that Nagender had suppressed material information in his affidavit and urged the court to declare his election as illegal and set it aside. title: FBI co-deputy director Andrew Bailey resigns after just over a year, says âreturning to family in Missouriâ
text: FBI co-deputy director Andrew Bailey FBI Co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey is stepping down from his post after just over a year at the US law enforcement agency, saying he is leaving to return to his family in Missouri. Bailey, a Republican ally of President Donald Trump, announced his resignation on Monday after joining the FBI from his position as Missouri attorney general. He served under FBI Director Kash Patel and was involved in investigations related to the 2020 US election. Writing on X (formerly Twitter), Bailey thanked Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Patel for the opportunity to serve at the FBI. âWith great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri,â Bailey wrote. He also expressed support for Patel, âI am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence.â Bailey was part of the FBI leadership overseeing day-to-day law enforcement operations. During his tenure, he helped manage the Trump administration's investigations into election-related issues and was present when FBI agents seized 2020 election ballots in Georgia earlier this year. The FBI has examined election records in several states but has not produced evidence supporting Trump's claims that widespread voter fraud caused his defeat in the 2020 presidential election. Bailey's departure comes about five weeks before the US midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress. The Trump administration has also stepped up federal investigations into voting by non-US citizens ahead of the elections. The FBI's deputy director position has traditionally been held by career bureau officials and was considered a non-political role. Under Trump, political allies have been appointed to senior positions as the administration seeks to reshape the agency. Bailey initially served as co-deputy director alongside Dan Bongino, a former US Secret Service agent and conservative podcaster. Bongino left the FBI in January. He joined the FBI amid scrutiny of Patel's leadership, including the bureau's handling of investigative files involving late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, which created political pressure for the Trump administration and tensions within the Justice Department. text: Chandigarh: The dispute over the delayed Panjab University Teachersâ Association (Puta) elections has intensified, with the association leadership questioning the validity of a faculty groupâs demand for an emergent general body meeting (GBM), even as the group has announced an extraordinary GBM on Oct 15. In a communication to Prof Parveen Goyal, Puta president Amarjit Singh Naura and secretary Mrityunjay Kumar said the Puta Constitution does not provide for an âEmergent General Body Meetingâ to be requisitioned in the manner mentioned in the faculty membersâ communication. The office-bearers cited Article 23 (IV) of the constitution, which states that an emergent meeting can be convened only when the president and secretary believe exceptional circumstances exist or an urgent matter requires immediate attention. Such a meeting may be called with a minimum notice period of five days. The response came in reference to a requisition dated Sept 18 and a subsequent reminder dated Sept 22 seeking an emergent GBM. The leadership also urged members to avoid attempts to âmisguide, confuse and divideâ the association. However, in a fresh communication issued on Oct 2, the requisitioning faculty members described the proposed meeting as an âExtraordinary General Body Meetingâ and announced that it would be held on Oct 15. The group said the requisition had the support of more than 40 faculty members and that reminders had been sent to the Puta president on Sept 22 and Sept 26. The proposed agenda includes announcement of a revised schedule for the Puta elections and appointment of a returning officer. The faculty members have relied on Article 23 (III) of the Puta Constitution, which provides for an extraordinary GBM on a written requisition signed by at least 40 members. Under the provision, the executive committee is required to convene the meeting within 15 working days of receiving the requisition. If it fails to do so, the requisitionists may themselves call the meeting after giving a further 10 daysâ notice, provided the required number of signatures remains intact. The differing interpretations of the constitution have added a fresh dimension to the ongoing controversy over the Puta election schedule, which has already run beyond the prescribed timeline. The MEA said Machchhar remained under âexcellent medical careâ and that it was in touch with his family and local authorities. We are in touch with his family & local authorities, extending support for a speedy recovery. Our thanks to UAE gov. for their care. We join well-wishers in praying for his good health,â Indian embassy in UAE said in a post on X. The attack took place on September 30 aboard flydubai flight FZ1073, which was bound for Tel Aviv. According to the UAE's state news agency WAM, citing attorney general counsellor Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, the Omani co-pilot, Hamam al-Hammami, attacked Machchhar with a cockpit crash axe while attempting to take control of the aircraft. Co-pilot allegedly tried to seize control The UAE attorney general said al-Hammami âattempted to carry out a terrorist actâ and sought to seize command of the aircraft's piloting instruments while the plane was airborne. The assault triggered a violent struggle inside the cockpit, during which the aircraft reportedly lost about 16,000 feet in two minutes, according to reports on the incident. Machchhar, despite sustaining serious injuries, fought back and managed to unlock the cockpit door. Crew members, passengers and two off-duty pilots then entered the cockpit and helped overpower the co-pilot, allowing the aircraft to be stabilised. The flight subsequently made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. All 180 people on board safely disembarked. A crash axe is a standard emergency tool kept in aircraft cockpits and is designed to help pilots cut through aircraft materials during emergencies. UAE investigation underway The UAE authorities are investigating the incident to establish the circumstances, motive and possible connections linked to the attack. âThe conclusive findings will be made public immediately once all mandatory legal and administrative steps have successfully concluded,â al-Shamsi said, according to WAM. title: Indian green card holder charged in Texas over illegal voting crackdown; 6 others also booked
text: Khalwinder Singh Bhengura was arrested on September 11 in US. A 69-year-old Indian Green Card holder is among seven non-citizens facing federal charges in Texas over alleged illegal voting or false claims of US citizenship. Khalwinder Singh Bhengura, an Indian man and lawful permanent resident since 2022, has been charged with voting by an alien in a federal election and making a false statement of citizenship to register to vote, according to the US Attorneyâs Office for the Northern District of Texas. Prosecutors allege Bhengura claimed to be a US citizen when registering to vote in January 2024. He allegedly made another citizenship claim while applying for a Texas driver's licence in August that year and later voted in the November 2024 general election. Authorities said Bhengura subsequently admitted that he knew he was not a US citizen. He was arrested on September 11. Bhengura is one of seven non-citizens charged as part of a federal investigation into voting and citizenship-related offences in North Texas. Six defendants were indicted on September 10, while another was charged through a criminal complaint the following day. Federal authorities said the arrests followed the charges. The other defendants include Nigerian nationals Helen Mayen Adams and Joshua Nmelichukwu Akpom, Mexican nationals Carlos Salas Barrios, Rocio Thrasher and Moises Anwar Arellano-Alba, and Celestin Katubadi, a citizen of the Democratic Republic of Congo. The cases differ. Prosecutors allege Adams, Barrios, Thrasher, Katubadi and Arellano-Alba were involved in voting-related offences or false claims of citizenship. Akpom faces a separate charge involving alleged false statements in a naturalisation application regarding previous claims of US citizenship, voter registration, and voting. In Bhenguraâs case, prosecutors allege the ballot was cast in Tarrant County during the November 2024 election. The federal case is being investigated by Homeland Security Investigations and the FBI Dallas field office, with assistance from the Texas Attorney Generalâs Election Integrity Unit and the Tarrant County District Attorneyâs Office. US Attorney Ryan Raybould said federal authorities would pursue cases involving non-citizens who vote in federal elections or falsely claim citizenship. âFederal elections belong to American citizensâperiod,â Raybould said, adding that the charges were intended to enforce federal election laws. HSI Dallas acting Deputy Special Agent in Charge Judy Pardo described election integrity as a national security priority, while FBI Dallas Special Agent in Charge R. Joseph Rothrock said the bureau would investigate allegations of voter fraud and other election crimes. The charges concern alleged conduct during the 2024 election cycle. title: California man arrested on charges of smuggling banned Nvidia chips to China; follows arrest of Super Micro Computer founder, may face 20 years in jail
text: Representative image A California man has been arrested over alleged chip smuggling. The 38-year-old owner of San Gabriel Valley-based Earthmade Computer Inc. is accused of smuggling more than $300 million worth of export-controlled computer servers containing US-manufactured graphics processing units (GPUs) to China. Prosecutors allege that Greg Lui, also known as âYiu Kong Luiâ, used false paperwork and routed the high-end servers through countries including Malaysia and Singapore before they were allegedly re-exported to China. The case follows US authorities' separate arrest of Super Micro Computer co-founder Yih-Shyan âWallyâ Liaw in connection with an alleged scheme to divert Nvidia-powered AI servers to China. If convicted of all three charges, Lui could face up to 20 years in prison on the conspiracy and money laundering counts and up to 10 years on the smuggling count. California man accused of smuggling Nvidia chips to China Lui is charged with one count of conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act and Export Administration Regulations, one count of outbound smuggling and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. âSI is the defining technology of the era,â said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. âThe National Security Division will protect the American advantage in the chips that power this technology, a product of our unparalleled innovation and hard work, from illegal diversion by our economic and military adversaries.â According to an indictment returned on Sept. 29, Lui allegedly used Earthmade to buy export-controlled items between 2023 and 2024 and send them to China without required US licences. Prosecutors allege that the equipment was first shipped to Malaysia and Singapore before being re-exported to China. They also allege that Lui provided false documentation to US manufacturers, misrepresenting the intended end users and destinations. From January to October 2024, Earthmade received more than $176 million from two Malaysia-based shipment companies as part of the alleged scheme. How the alleged scheme worked In January 2024, Lui allegedly emailed a conspirator about a Malaysian transshipment company seeking 70 servers with export-restricted GPUs. Later that month, he allegedly ordered 27 servers from a US manufacturer for approximately $7.614 million. The servers were shipped from Los Angeles to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, with documents identifying their GPUs as export-controlled equipment that could not be sent to China without a licence. In March 2024, a co-conspirator allegedly told a Malaysian government official that the 27 servers had been transshipped to a China-based buyer. âProtecting Americaâs national security means keeping our advanced Super Intelligence technology from being used to strengthen our adversariesâ military capabilities,â said First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. âThis defendant allegedly used false paperwork and shipments through third countries to smuggle more than $300 million in export-controlled computer servers to China. We will aggressively prosecute those who put our national security at risk for profit.â FBI warns over advanced AI technology âThe FBIâs investigation revealed that Lui allegedly sold the Chinese government hundreds of millions of dollarsâ worth of American Super Intelligence technology, in clear violation of U.S. export control laws,â said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBIâs Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. âControlling the export of advanced SI technology is critical to safeguarding our national security and defending the homeland, and the FBI will keep fighting for Americaâs businesses and economic security. Weâre grateful to our partners across the U.S. government and private sector for their assistance, and weâll continue holding accountable anyone who violates U.S. export laws to enrich themselves and help our adversaries.â âPreventing the illegal export of controlled technology is critical to protecting our national security,â said Special Agent in Charge John E. Helsing of the Department of Defense Office of Inspector General Defense Criminal Investigative Service (DCIS) Western Field Office. âThese technologies provide core advantages to U.S. forces, and ensuring they remain safeguarded prevents adversaries from exploiting them. Todayâs action underscores our commitment to protecting advanced defense capabilities and enforcing the laws that keep them out of the hands of those who may threaten the United States.â Lui could face up to 20 years in prison If convicted of all charges, Lui could face a maximum of 20 years in prison on the conspiracy count, 20 years on the money laundering count and 10 years on the smuggling count. title: 391 electrocuted in MP in 2025-26, 26% higher than last year
text: Bhopal: 391 persons died due to electrocution-related cases and accidents in 2025-26 in MP, with both accidents and fatalities rising from the previous year, as per the Union ministry of powerâs Central Electricity Authority (CEA) data. 310 people were killed in 2024-25, marking a 26% jump in deaths in 2025-26. The state recorded 668 electrical accidents in 2025-26. In 2024-25, it reported 619 accidents, including 310 human fatalities. Data from the CEAâs Electrical Accident Data Monitoring System (EADMS) also places MP among states reporting a high number of electrical fatalities. Maharashtra recorded the highest number of human deaths in 2025-26 at 1,702, followed by Uttar Pradesh (1,174), Andhra Pradesh (1,111), Gujarat (656), Karnataka (501) and Madhya Pradesh (391). Falling electric poles and snapping high-tension wires caused 46 human and 67 animal deaths in MP in 2025-26, compared with 37 human and 80 animal deaths in 2024-25. The issue has come into focus following the death of 30-year-old Divyarishi Tiwari in Bhopal on Sunday night. Tiwari, a BJYM district general secretary and advocate, was allegedly electrocuted after coming into contact with a live wire tied to an electric pole while crossing a road divider near a mall in MP Nagar. The incident has raised concerns about electrical safety at pedestrian cut points, particularly those used for informal road crossings. Several such points in the city are close to electrical installations, potentially exposing pedestrians to hazards from poles, damaged or exposed wiring and other electrical infrastructure. It has also drawn attention to the wider safety concern at locations where road dividers, pedestrian crossing points and electrical infrastructure are close together. title: 2 Indians charged in US for smuggling fake Ozempic from China
text: Swapnadip Roy and Vicky Ramancha charged in US for smuggling fake Ozempic from China. Two Indian nationals have been charged in the United States for allegedly smuggling counterfeit Ozempic, a weight-loss drug, from China and selling the products to distributors in the country, the Department of Justice said Tuesday. Swapnadip Roy, 33, and Vicky Ramancha, 37, were charged in the Middle District of Florida. Roy was extradited from Italy to the US and made his initial appearance in Tampa on Tuesday, where he pleaded not guilty. Ramancha remains at large. Prosecutors allege that Roy and Ramancha obtained counterfeit Ozempic in China between July 2023 and April 2024 and sold the products to US distributors at discounted prices. The counterfeit products allegedly included packaging, package inserts, pen labels and needles designed to make buyers believe they were purchasing genuine Ozempic authorised by the manufacturer. The alleged scheme continued even after the US Food and Drug Administration seized some of the counterfeit Ozempic in December 2023 and issued a public warning about the products, the department said. Roy and Ramancha are charged with one count of conspiracy to commit smuggling and defraud the United States, three counts of smuggling, and two counts of selling counterfeit drugs and holding counterfeit drugs for sale. If convicted, each faces a maximum sentence of 71 years in prison. Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department's Criminal Division said counterfeit prescription drugs pose a threat to people who depend on the safety of the pharmaceutical supply. âThese defendants allegedly exploited peopleâs health to pay themselves. We will keep pursuing anyone who seeks to deceive American consumers with counterfeit drugs,â Duva said. Assistant US Attorney Christopher Murray for the Middle District of Florida said the indictment reflected the department's efforts to protect Americans from potential harm caused by counterfeit prescription drugs. The FDA's Office of Criminal Investigations is investigating the case. Assistant Commissioner Justin Green said introducing counterfeit drugs into the US pharmaceutical supply chain puts consumers at significant risk. Roy was arrested in Italy pursuant to an INTERPOL Red Notice before the Justice Department secured his continued detention and sought his extradition to the US. You use AI every day. title: Senate revival sharpens poll debate
text: Students of Utkal University on Aug 25 submitted memorandum to chief minister Mohan Charan Majhi through the instituteâs vicechancellor Chandi Prasad Nanda, demanding campus elections The revival of university Senates has added a fresh dimension to Odishaâs prolonged debate over studentsâ union elections, with the amended university law providing for elected student leaders to be part of the Senate even as campuses remain without regular union polls. The Odisha Universities (Amendment) Act, 2024, which came into force in April 2025, restored the Senate after the previous BJD govt abolished it in 2020, arguing that the body had become âornamentalâ. The Senate is a key university authority dealing with academics, research, resources, accounts and financial management, among other matters. Significantly, the amended law provides for the president and secretary of the university studentsâ union to be Senate members. In the absence of elected unions, however, universities have had to find alternatives. A vice-chancellor of a state public university said two students are currently selected from PG departments on merit and included as Senate members. âBut that leaves them with little role to play in the functioning of the Senate,â he said. At the same time, universities remain wary of the violence and disruption historically associated with direct polls. Utkal University, Ravenshaw University and other campuses have witnessed election-related unrest in the past. Academics have consequently suggested alternative models, including indirect elections, to retain student representation while reducing the scope for violence and outside political interference. With the govt yet to announce a schedule, student organisations are preparing to step up pressure. BCJD president Ipsita Sahu said the organisation was planning district-wise agitations and would gherao the higher education ministerâs residence and the assembly if the govt continued to delay the elections. ABVP member Bishwajit Patra said the organisation had consistently demanded restoration of student polls and had also filed a PIL in the Orissa high court. NSUI too has indicated plans to intensify its agitation over the delay.
